title: magnitudedev/magnitude — Open source inference engine for agents that optimizes itself for your exact hardware. Compiles and tunes its kernels on your device, so open models run up to 2x faster than llama.cpp. Works on Apple Silicon, NVIDIA, AMD, or just a CPU.
content:
Run open models as fast as your hardware allows
Magnitude is an open source inference engine for agents that optimizes itself for your exact hardware. It compiles and tunes its kernels on your device, so open models run up to 2x faster than llama.cpp. One click connects the agent you already use (Pi, OpenCode, Hermes, Codex, and more). Works on Apple Silicon, NVIDIA, AMD, or nothing but a CPU.
Download Magnitude for macOS, Windows, or Linux
⭐ Help us reach more developers and grow the Magnitude community. Star this repo!
demo-9-29.mp4
- Download Magnitude, install it, and open the app.
- Choose a recommended model in Discover and download it.
- Connect your agent in Connections and start using it.
The desktop app includes the magnitude CLI. No separate installation is needed.
- Up to 2x faster than llama.cpp: 92% faster decode on Metal, 19% on CUDA
- Tuned on your device: kernels are tuned on your hardware before a model runs
- Built for the best models: hand-optimized kernels for popular open-weight families
- Memory that flexes: 27% less memory per agent, freed when agents stop
- Fast concurrent sessions: sessions share prefix caches to prevent slowdown
- Works with your agent: one click to connect Pi, OpenCode, Hermes, Codex, and more
- Free, private, open source: no token costs, nothing leaves your machine, Apache 2.0
An open source inference engine that optimizes itself for your hardware. It ships as a desktop app that runs open models and connects them to the agent you already use.
They ship kernels precompiled for broad classes of hardware. Magnitude compiles and tunes its kernels on your actual device before a model runs, so they fit your exact chip. See the benchmarks against llama.cpp.
Any Apple Silicon, NVIDIA, or AMD GPU, or nothing but a CPU. There is no fixed minimum. Smaller machines run smaller models, and more memory lets you run larger ones.
macOS, Linux, and Windows.

report.summary: Magnitude, an open-source inference engine, compiles and tunes kernels on your own hardware, claiming up to 2x faster open-model inference than llama.cpp across Apple Silicon, NVIDIA, AMD, and CPU.
report.background: Local LLM inference has long been dominated by llama.cpp and its GGML kernels, which ship precompiled for broad hardware classes — a generalist tradeoff that leaves real performance on the table. Meanwhile, coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Cline have driven demand for fast, private, locally hosted models. Rivals such as vLLM, SGLang, MLX, Ollama, and LM Studio mostly target datacenter GPUs or fixed Apple Silicon paths. Magnitude's bet is just-in-time kernel compilation and autotuning on the user's exact chip, combined with agent-oriented features like shared prefix caches across concurrent sessions and per-agent memory reclamation. It ships as an Apache 2.0 desktop app with a bundled CLI, no token costs, and fully offline operation once a model is downloaded.
key_points: Device-specific kernel compilation: instead of shipping precompiled kernels for broad hardware classes, Magnitude compiles and autotunes kernels on your actual machine before a model runs. The project reports this yields 92% faster decoding on Metal and 19% on CUDA versus llama.cpp, with an overall claim of up to 2x speedups.

Hardware breadth and low floor: it runs on any Apple Silicon, NVIDIA, or AMD GPU, or on CPU alone, with no fixed minimum spec. Smaller machines simply run smaller models, while more unified or discrete memory lets you serve larger ones. macOS, Linux, and Windows are supported.

Built for agents, not just chat: one-click connections cover Pi, OpenCode, Hermes, OpenClaw, Codex, Claude Code, Oh My Pi, and Cline, with any other tool working through an OpenAI-compatible API. Concurrent sessions share prefix caches to avoid the slowdown typical when multiple agents hit one local model.

Memory and privacy posture: the engine claims 27% less memory per agent and frees that memory when agents stop. Everything — prompts, files, models — stays on your machine, and no internet is needed after a model is downloaded. Licensed Apache 2.0 with no token costs.

Deliberately narrow model support: rather than being a generalist runtime, Magnitude hand-writes optimized kernels for the most popular open-weight families. That focus is presented as the source of its performance edge, but it also means the fastest path exists only for models the team has explicitly tuned.
report.impact: If the benchmarks hold outside vendor testing, Magnitude pressures the local-inference status quo: llama.cpp's generalist kernel strategy and Ollama/LM Studio's convenience-first packaging. For the AI industry, it reinforces a trend toward per-device autotuning and agent-aware serving rather than one-size-fits-all runtimes, mirroring what vLLM and SGLang did for datacenter GPUs. For developers, faster decode and shared prefix caches make multi-agent workflows on a single workstation genuinely practical, cutting cloud token spend. For regular users, the bigger win is privacy: a desktop app, offline operation, and no data leaving the machine. Caveats remain — first-run tuning costs, a limited model list, and self-reported speedups that need independent replication.
report.tools: To compare or follow up: llama.cpp and Ollama for the baseline most users already run; LM Studio for a GUI alternative; MLX for Apple Silicon-native experimentation; vLLM and SGLang for server-side serving; and Jan or text-generation-webui for local front-ends. Magnitude itself ships a desktop app plus CLI at github.com/magnitudedev/magnitude, with the model list at magnitude.dev/models. Running the same model in llama.cpp and Magnitude on your own hardware is the fastest way to validate the 2x claim.
